source_text: Ecclesiae quidem ueritate epistolam istam ad Ephesios habemus emissam, non ad Laodicenos; sed Marcion et titulum aliquando interpolare gestit, quasi et in isto diligentissimus explorator. nihil autem de titulis interest, cum ad omnes apostolus scripserit dum ad quosdam, certe tamen eum deum praedicans in Christo, cui competunt quae praedicantur. cui ergo competet secundum boni existimationem, quam proposuerit in sacramento uoluntatis suae, in dispensationem adimpletionis temporum — ut ita dixerim, sicut uerbum illud in Graeco sonat — recapitulare — id est ad initium redigere uel ab initio recensere — omnia in Christum, quae in caelis et quae in terrisnisi cuius erunt omnia ab initio, etiam ipsum initium, a quo et tempora et temporum adimple(tio et adimple)tionis dispensatio, ob quam omnia ad initium recensentur in Christo? alterius autem dei quod initium, id est unde, cuius opus nullum? quae tempora sine initio? quae adimpletio sine temporibus? quae dispensatio sine adimpletione? denique quid in terris egit iam olim, ut longa aliqua temporum adimplendorum dispensatio reputetur ad recensenda omnia in Christo, etiam quae in caelis? nec in caelis autem res ab altero actas existimabimus, quaecumque sunt, quam ab eo, a quo et in terris actas omnibus constat. quodsi non capit alterius <omnia) ista deputari ab initio quam creatoris, quis credet ab alio ea recenseri in Christum alium, et non a suo auctore et in suum Christum? si creatoris sunt, diuersa sint necesse est a diuerso deo; si diuersa, utique contraria. quomodo ergo contraria recenseantur in eum, a quo denique destruuntur? nam et sequentia quem renuntiant Christum, cum dicit: ut simus in laudem gloriae (eius) nos, qui praesperauimus in Christum? qui enim praesperasse potuerunt, id est ante sperasse in deum quam uenisset, nisi Iudaei, quibus Christus praenuntiabatur ab initio? qui ergo praenuntiabatur, ille et praesperabatur. atque adeo hoc ad se, id est ad Iudaeos, refert, ut distinctionem faciat conuersus ad nationes: in quo et uos, cum audissetis sermonem ueritatis, euangelium, in quo credidistis et signati estis spiritu promissionis eius sancto. cuius promissionis? factae per Iohelem: in nouissimis diebus effundam de meo spiritu in omnem carnem, id est et in nationes. ita (et) spiritus et euangelium in eo erit Christo, qui praesperabatur, dum praedicabatur. Sed et 'pater gloriae\' ille est, cuius Christus rex gloriae canitur in psalmo ascendens: quis est iste rex gloriae? dominus uirtutum ipse est rex gloriae; ab illo \'spiritus sapientiae\' optatur, apud quem haec quoque spiritalium species enumeratur inter septem spiritus per Esaiam; ille dabit (inluminatos cordis oculos\', qui etiam exteriores oculos luce ditauit, cui displicet caecitas populi: et quis caecus nisi pueri mei? et excaecati sunt famuli dei; apud illum sunt et \'diuitiae hereditatis in sanctis\'. qui eam hereditatem ex uocatione nationum repromisit: postula de me, et dabo tibi gentes hereditatem tuam; ille \'inoperatus est in Christum ualentiam suam suscitando eum a mortuis et collocando eum ad dexteram suam subiciendo omnia\', qui et dixit:
pass_a_gloss: Indeed we have the epistle to the Ephesians emitted by the truth of the Church, not to the Laodiceans; but Marcion also sometimes endeavors to interpolate the title, as if he were a very diligent investigator in this matter. However, nothing is of interest regarding the titles, since the apostle wrote to all while writing to some, certainly preaching God in Christ, to whom belong the things that are preached. To whom, therefore, will it belong, according to the estimation of good, which he proposed in the sacrament of his will, in the dispensation of the fulfillment of times - so to speak, as that word sounds in Greek - to recapitulate, that is, to reduce to the beginning or to recount from the beginning, all things in Christ, which are in heaven and which are on earth, if not to him whose are all things from the beginning, and even the beginning itself, from which are also the times and the dispensation of the fulfillment of times, on account of which all things are recounted in Christ? What beginning, that is, from where, does the work of another god have? What times without a beginning? What fulfillment without times? What dispensation without fulfillment? Finally, what has he done on earth, so that a long dispensation of fulfilling times may be reckoned to recount all things in Christ, even those in heaven? Nor will we consider that things done in heaven are from another, whatever they are, than from him, from whom it is agreed that all things done on earth are. But if these things cannot be assigned to another from the beginning, except to the Creator, who will believe that they are recounted in another Christ, and not by his own author and in his own Christ? If they are the Creator's, they must necessarily be different from those of a different god; if different, certainly contrary. How, therefore, can contrary things be recounted in him, from whom they are finally destroyed? For also the following words declare Christ, when he says: so that we may be to the praise of his glory, we who have hoped beforehand in Christ. For who could have hoped beforehand, that is, hoped in God before he came, except the Jews, to whom Christ was announced from the beginning? He, therefore, who was announced, was also hoped for beforehand. And so this refers to them, that is, to the Jews, so as to make a distinction, turning to the nations: in which also you, when you heard the word of truth, the gospel, in which you believed and were sealed with the Holy Spirit of his promise. Whose promise? The one made through Joel: in the last days I will pour out my Spirit on all flesh, that is, also on the nations. So both the Spirit and the gospel will be in Christ, who was hoped for beforehand, while he was being preached. But also 'the Father of glory' is he, whose Christ, the King of glory, is sung in the psalm, ascending: who is this King of glory? The Lord of hosts, he is the King of glory; from him the 'Spirit of wisdom' is sought, with whom also these species of spiritual things are enumerated among the seven spirits through Isaiah; he will give 'enlightened eyes of the heart', who also enriched the outer eyes with light, to whom the blindness of the people is displeasing: and who is blind, if not my children? And the servants of God were blinded; with him are also 'the riches of the inheritance in the saints'. He promised this inheritance from the calling of the nations: ask of me, and I will give you the nations as your inheritance; he 'worked in Christ, raising him from the dead and placing him at his right hand, subjecting all things', who also said:

pass_b_english: We possess the epistle to the Ephesians on the authority of the Church's truth, not an epistle to the Laodiceans; yet Marcion sometimes tries to tamper with the title, acting as if he were a supremely diligent investigator in this matter. But the title is of no consequence, since the apostle wrote to all while writing to some, certainly preaching God in Christ, to whom belong the things that are preached. To whom, then, will it belong—according to the good purpose he set forth in the mystery of his will, in the administration of the fullness of times, to use the Greek term, to recapitulate (that is, to bring back to the beginning or to recount from the beginning) all things in Christ, both those in heaven and those on earth—if not to him whose are all things from the beginning, and even the beginning itself, from which also come the times and the administration of the fullness of times, on account of which all things are recounted in Christ? (Ephesians 1:10) What beginning—that is, from where—does another god's work have? What times without a beginning? What fulfillment without times? What administration without fulfillment? Finally, what did he do on earth long ago, so that a long administration of times to be fulfilled might be reckoned for the purpose of recounting all things in Christ, even those in heaven? Nor will we suppose that things done in heaven, whatever they are, were acted by another than the one from whom it is agreed all things done on earth proceed. But if these things cannot be assigned to another from the beginning except to the Creator, who will believe they are recounted in another Christ, and not by his own author and in his own Christ? If they are the Creator's, they must necessarily differ from those of a different god; if they differ, they are certainly contrary. How then can contrary things be recounted in him by whom they are finally destroyed? For the following words also declare Christ, when he says: 'so that we might be to the praise of his glory, we who first hoped in Christ' (Ephesians 1:12). For who could have hoped beforehand—that is, hoped in God before he came—except the Jews, to whom Christ was announced from the beginning? Therefore, he who was announced was also hoped for beforehand. And so this refers to them, that is, to the Jews, in order to make a distinction, turning to the nations: 'in whom you also, when you heard the word of truth, the gospel of your salvation, and believed in him, were sealed with the promised Holy Spirit' (Ephesians 1:13). Whose promise? The one made through Joel: 'In the last days I will pour out my Spirit on all flesh'—that is, also on the nations (Joel 2:28). Thus both the Spirit and the gospel will be in Christ, who was hoped for beforehand while he was being preached. But 'the Father of glory' is also he whose Christ, the King of glory, is sung in the psalm ascending: 'Who is this King of glory? The Lord of hosts, he is the King of glory' (Psalm 24:10); from him the 'Spirit of wisdom' is sought, with whom these species of spiritual gifts are also enumerated among the seven spirits through Isaiah; he will give 'enlightened eyes of the heart' (Ephesians 1:18), who also enriched the outer eyes with light, to whom the blindness of the people is displeasing: 'and who is blind but my children? And the servants of God were blinded' (Isaiah 42:19); with him are also 'the riches of his glorious inheritance in the saints' (Ephesians 1:18). He promised this inheritance from the calling of the nations: 'Ask of me, and I will make the nations your heritage' (Psalm 2:8); he 'worked in Christ, raising him from the dead and seating him at his right hand, subjecting all things' (Ephesians 1:20–22), who also said:
